item.title: Measuring Research Convergence in Interdisciplinary Teams Using Large Language Models and Graph Analytics
item.description:
Wenwen Li, Yuanyuan Tian, Sizhe Wang, Amber Wutich, Paul Westerhoff, Sarah Porter, Anais Roque, Mohammad Jobayer Hossain, et al.
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70459
ABSTRACT Understanding how interdisciplinary research teams converge on shared knowledge is a persistent challenge. This paper presents a novel, multi‐layer, AI‐driven analytical framework for mapping research convergence in interdisciplinary teams. The framework integrates large language models (LLMs), graph‐based visualization and analytics, and human‐in‐the‐loop evaluation to examine how research viewpoints are shared, influenced, and integrated over time. LLMs are used to extract structured viewpoints aligned with the Needs–Approach–Benefits–Competition (NABC) framework and to infer potential viewpoint flows across presenters, forming a common semantic foundation for three complementary analyses: (1) similarity‐based qualitative analysis to identify two key types of viewpoints, popular and unique, for building convergence, (2) quantitative cross‐domain influence analysis using network centrality measures, and (3) temporal viewpoint flow analysis to capture convergence dynamics. To address uncertainty in LLM‐based inference, the framework incorporates expert validation through structured surveys and cross‐layer consistency checks. A case study on water insecurity in underserved communities as part of the Arizona Water Innovation Initiatives demonstrates increasing viewpoint convergence and domain‐specific influence patterns, illustrating the value of the proposed AI‐enabled approach for research convergence analysis.

item.title: Behavior‐Oriented Inference of Trip Purposes and Urban Mobility Structures From Dockless Bike‐Sharing Data
item.description:
Sirui Wei, Zihan Kan, Yan Liu, Haiyan Hao, Dong Liu
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70445
ABSTRACT Dockless bike‐sharing systems generate large volumes of passively collected mobility data, creating new opportunities for understanding urban activity patterns and travel behavior. However, inferring trip purposes from dockless bike‐sharing data remains challenging due to the absence of explicit activity labels and the complexity of mixed‐use urban environments. Using dockless bike‐sharing trip records from 11 sampled days in 2021 in Shenzhen, China, we develop a behavior‐oriented framework for inferring trip purposes by integrating gravity models with Bayesian rules, functional land use, temporal preference, and nighttime light intensity. The inferred results reveal highly interpretable spatiotemporal mobility structures, including pronounced weekday commuting rhythms, mixed‐use intra‐category circulation, and strong functional interactions among home, work, schooling, and transfer‐related activities. To further examine mixed‐use urban mobility behaviors, a semantic adjustment strategy and post hoc activity‐chain exploration are introduced, providing alternative interpretations of mixed‐purpose movements and plausible record‐linked sequential activity patterns embedded within cycling trips. Our results further demonstrate strong temporal consistency and high spatial replicability under machine learning approximation, indicating that the inferred behavioral structures capture stable and reproducible spatiotemporal regularities that can be learned across dates. These findings show that even under incomplete and weakly supervised mobility data conditions, dockless bike‐sharing trips contain reproducible behavioral structures that can support interpretable urban activity analysis, providing new opportunities for behavior‐oriented mobility analysis in data‐scarce urban environments.

item.title: Measuring Ridership Changes During a Fare‐Free Policy Using Large‐Scale Mobile App Data and Explainable Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
Luyu Liu, Harvey J. Miller
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70460
ABSTRACT Fare‐free policies are reported to improve transit affordability and ridership, yet their high‐resolution spatial and temporal effects remain poorly understood. This study examines ridership changes during the Central Ohio Transit Authority's systemwide fare suspension from March 2020 to January 2021. We developed a two‐model explainable artificial intelligence‐driven framework with Automatic Passenger Counter records and large‐scale mobile app usage data. A Poisson histogram gradient boosting model estimated counterfactual fare‐paying benchmark ridership, while a random forest model with Shapley Additive Explanations identified factors associated with excess ridership. Observed ridership exceeded the counterfactual benchmark by 28.1% overall and by 56.9% during May–August, with substantial variation across neighborhoods and policy phases. Higher excess ridership was associated with greater service, closer transit access, lower income, lower vehicle ownership, fewer remote‐work occupations, higher poverty, and larger Black population shares. Transit agencies can use the framework to identify spatial and temporal patterns of excess ridership and associated factors to inform the coordination of fare policies with service and accessibility investments.

item.title: Discovering Governing Spatial Interaction Equations in Dynamic Urban Systems
item.description:
Zhongfu Ma, Di Zhu
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70441
ABSTRACT Governing equations are fundamental for describing and predicting dynamic urban geographic systems. Unlike physical systems guided by first principles, urban spatiotemporal phenomena emerge from coupled geographic processes that lack deterministic theoretical foundations, making the discovery of governing equations elusive and largely heuristic. Spatiotemporal dynamics in urban systems are often observed as sequential snapshots of spatial distribution, while the spatial interactions, or the flows, that cause such dynamics are often implied or unknown. In this study, we propose a general differential equation formalism that decomposes urban dynamics into a spatial interaction process and a self‐dynamic component. Building on this formalism, we introduce the Urban Discovery Framework (U‐Discovery), which integrates hypothesis generation, neural fitting, and governing equation identification for discovering the governing equations of spatial interaction. U‐Discovery leverages Large Language Models and literature‐based reasoning to propose differential equation candidates. Each candidate is calibrated from the observed spatiotemporal dynamics using a neural fitting method. The candidates are evaluated and ranked based on the fitting error and mathematical complexity. A synthetic experiment using simulated dynamics demonstrates that U‐Discovery can identify the governing equation from a candidate set. Empirical experiments examine real‐world active population dynamics in Hennepin County, Minnesota. Drawing on both literature‐derived scientific priors and broader knowledge from LLMs, U‐Discovery proposes original candidate equations and identifies those that best reproduce observed population dynamics. The discovered equations show an ability to recover the underlying mobility flows, while their varying performance across spatial scales suggests that different interaction mechanisms may dominate at different scales.

item.title: An Iterative Framework for Extracting Nested Spatial Relation Patterns From Geoscience Texts
item.description:
Deping Chu, Siwen Chen, Bo Wan, Fang Fang, Shunping Zhou, Wei Luo, Lin Yang
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70457
ABSTRACT Spatial relation extraction (SRE) aimed to identify spatial relations such as direction and topology between entities described in text. However, existing methods overlook the recognition of nested spatial relation patterns, in which one spatial relation may contain another complete spatial relation unit. To address this limitation, we introduce Geo‐RE, a novel framework designed to iteratively extract nested spatial relation patterns by effectively integrating both semantic and structural information from geoscience terms. Our approach leverages the pre‐trained language model Geo‐BERT, which captures the rich contextual semantic information specific to geoscience texts. Additionally, a convolutional neural network (CNN) is employed to extract radical features of Chinese words, which aids in identifying structural and semantic characteristics unique to geoscience terminology. During the iterative hierarchical extraction process, a candidate relation triple filtering mechanism is designed to eliminate semantically or physically invalid relations, thereby ensuring identification efficiency and accuracy. Finally, a hierarchical neural network is adopted to iteratively identify nested spatial relation patterns in a layer‐by‐layer fashion. Experimental results on both the Policy dataset and our proprietary GeoRED dataset demonstrate that Geo‐RE achieves an optimal F1‐score of 88.10% on GeoRED and performs comparably to state‐of‐the‐art models on the Policy dataset.

item.title: A Density‐Adaptive, Cloud‐Oriented Framework for Fine‐Grained Object Recognition in Large‐Scale Multimodal Urban LiDAR
item.description:
Rytis Maskeliūnas, Sarmad Maqsood, Mantas Vaškevičius, Julius Gelšvartas
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70442
ABSTRACT National‐scale urban LiDAR datasets challenge conventional monolithic processing workflows because of their large volume, multimodal heterogeneity, and spatially non‐uniform point density, making scalable architectures that jointly exploit geometric, spectral, and geospatial contextual information essential for fine‐grained recognition. This study develops and evaluates a density‐adaptive, parameter‐efficient, cloud‐oriented extension for scalable tile‐based fine‐grained object recognition in large‐scale multimodal urban LiDAR data. The proposed coarse‐to‐fine pipeline integrates aerial LiDAR‐derived layers, RGB orthophotos, and OpenStreetMap priors into geo‐consistent 512 × 512 raster tiles with 3‐, 6‐, or 9‐channel inputs. RandLA‐Net and SegFormer provide coarse semantic segmentation, while a lightweight 3.8‐million‐parameter YOLOv11‐based detector identifies benches, poles, and traffic signs. To address non‐uniform LiDAR sampling, a per‐pixel density map is used for preprocessing control and adaptive selection of the DBSCAN neighborhood radius, followed by RANSAC‐based geometric filtering. The deployment design further organizes stateless tile‐processing jobs within a fault‐tolerant, horizontally scalable cloud architecture. Evaluation on more than 3.1 billion LiDAR points from Estonian urban areas showed that the full 9‐channel configuration improved scene mIoU by 10.7 percentage points and micro‐object recall by 16.4 percentage points compared with RGB‐only input. Under a unified comparison protocol, the proposed detector achieved 79.1% micro‐object F1 and 86.9% scene mIoU, outperforming the 35‐million‐parameter BEVFusion baseline, which achieved 76.3% and 86.1%, respectively. Density‐stratified experiments further demonstrated stable performance across varying point‐density conditions, while analytical projections based on the measured single‐node runtime indicated favorable horizontal scaling under the stated orchestration and I/O‐overhead assumptions. These findings demonstrate that controlled multimodal fusion, density‐adaptive refinement, and coarse‐to‐fine processing provide an accurate and computationally efficient foundation for national‐scale urban LiDAR analytics, supporting scalable smart‐city mapping, infrastructure monitoring, and urban planning applications.

item.title: A Question‐Answering Framework for Geoscientific Operator Retrieval Based on Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs
item.description:
Mingda Zhang, Zhiwei Liang, Qian Yang, Rong Li, LiLong Wu
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70456
ABSTRACT The widespread use of GIS technology has led to the development of many open‐source geoinformation tools, such as QGIS and GRASS GIS. Users often find it hard to locate the right operators and access knowledge on different platforms. Large language models (LLMs) are good at natural language tasks but are less accurate in specialized domains. To address this, we propose a question‐answering framework for geoscientific operators. This framework combines LLMs with Graph‐based Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (GraphRAG), which increases the precision and relevance of operator retrieval. We organize geoscientific algorithms and operator details in a structured Geoscientific Operator Knowledge Graph (GeoOpKG). This structure enables efficient retrieval through multi‐relational context encoding with Relational Graph Convolutional Networks (R‐GCN) and Cross‐Encoder re‐ranking. LLMs improve fluency and reasoning, making question‐answering more reliable. Experiments show our approach achieves higher precision than other LLM‐based systems for known, similar, and unknown operator queries. The framework raises retrieval precision and answer reliability, helping users understand and access geoscientific operator knowledge.
